corrected_value.title: Assessment of household food waste in Hungary

decisions.quote: The actual study is a replication of the first Hungarian measurement-based research conducted in 2016 [24], which we regarded as a baseline for comparison.
decisions.reason: The shipped original (Sotiropoulos et al., 2016, 10.1504/ijewm.2016.078598) is not cited in the paper and resulted from a metadata matching error on '2016' and 'household food waste'. The paper explicitly states that it is a replication of the 2016 Hungarian measurement-based household food waste study cited as reference [24], which is Szabó-Bódi, B.; Kasza, G.; Szakos, D. (2018), 'Assessment of household food waste in Hungary', Br. Food J., 120, 625-638 (DOI: 10.1108/BFJ-04-2017-0255), matching blind target 0. FUSIONS [38] is cited only as the standardized measurement methodology, and conference proceedings [45-47] or overview [44] are secondary dissemination works rather than the primary baseline study [24] compared in Table 5.

decisions.quote: The actual study is a replication of the first Hungarian measurement-based research conducted in 2016 [24], which we regarded as a baseline for comparison. A decrease of 4% in the annual food waste per capita estimation was observed between the two periods (65.49 kg compared to 68.04 kg from 2016). The constitution of food waste in the households was found to be very similar, indicating a dominant rate of avoidable food waste (an actual share of 48.82% compared to 48.70% in 2016), followed by the unavoidable part (47.05% compared to 47.13% in 2016). Potentially avoidable food waste remained under 5% in both periods. (Table 5).
decisions.reason: With the dependent original identity resolved to Szabó-Bódi et al. (2018) [24] (the same 2016 baseline referenced by the shipped outcome quote), the authors directly compare their 2019 household measurements to the 2016 study [24] and report very similar category proportions (avoidable 48.82% vs. 48.70%, unavoidable 47.05% vs. 47.13%, potentially avoidable 4.15% vs. 4.16%), the exact same order of the five most frequently discarded avoidable food types (meals, bakery products, fresh vegetables, dairy products, and fresh fruits; line 78), and a modest 4% decrease in total per capita waste interpreted as awareness campaign progress. Both shipped and blind correctly coded the replication outcome as 'successful'.

decisions.quote: The aim of this research was to estimate the amount of food waste that an average Hungarian household generates based on a one-week period. This investigation was a replication of a household food waste measurement conducted in 2016 with the same methodology, within the boundaries of the Wasteless (Maradék nélkül) food waste prevention campaign, organized by the National Food Chain Safety Office in Hungary.
decisions.reason: The study collected new primary physical measurement diary data from a fresh sample of 165 Hungarian households in 2019 using the same methodology to repeat and compare against the 2016 Hungarian household food waste study [24]. Both shipped and blind correctly coded the record type as 'replication'.
